Usage-based AI exposure across Australia’s earnings distribution

Mapping US task-usage data onto ANZSCO occupations

Author

Luc Taya, Economics (Honours) graduate, University of Western Australia

Published

25 October 2026

Important

Working draft, not for citation. Descriptive; not a job-loss or career-risk score; not advice.

The data behind this note are US task-level Claude.ai use by self-selected users, from one product. No Australian occupational AI use is measured. The usage-based exposure scores describe tasks in US occupations; this note applies them to the mix of occupations in Australian employment. Where the source data have Australian rows, those rows classify the task in a conversation, not the user’s job. Every result is shown beside at least one measure that does not come from Anthropic.

1 Question and framing

2 Data

Usage-based exposure. The measure is Massenkoff and McCrory’s “observed exposure” (Massenkoff and McCrory 2026), published as job_exposure.csv in the Anthropic Economic Index dataset (Massenkoff et al. 2026). It gives one score for each US occupation at the six-digit level of the SOC 2018 classification. The file has 756 rows. Of these, 411 (54%) are exactly zero; the mean is 0.077 and the maximum 0.745. Another 111 of the 867 detailed SOC occupations have no row, and these are treated as missing, not zero.

The score is built in steps, which matter for reading it:

  • Each O*NET task is first gated on use. A task counts only if its work-related Claude.ai conversations plus all first-party API calls reach a fixed count in Anthropic’s samples.
  • It is then gated on capability: the task must have an Eloundou et al. beta above zero (Eloundou et al. 2024).
  • Tasks that pass both gates are weighted between one half (augmentation only) and one (automation only).
  • The job score is the time-share-weighted sum over the job’s tasks.

So a zero means the job’s tasks fell below the usage gate, or that none of its used tasks passed the capability gate. It does not mean no use at all. Zeros are flagged as “below usage threshold” wherever unit values are shown. The conversations are classified into US O*NET tasks, and the samples are global Claude.ai and API traffic, not Australian.

Australian usage composition. For the comparison of usage with employment by occupation group (Section 4.6), the note uses the 2026-06-26 release of the AEI geography file. It covers Claude.ai conversations in 2 months, with 11,629 rows for Australia and 1,172 for Western Australia. For countries and subregions, detailed SOC rows are published only as shares of conversations. Collaboration measures, such as the automation share, exist for countries only at the SOC major-group level. Missing rows mean the cell was not published, not that it was zero.

Potential exposure. Three comparison measures do not depend on Claude.ai use:

  • Jobs and Skills Australia’s automation and augmentation exposure scores for ANZSCO unit groups (Jobs and Skills Australia 2025), available for 357 unit groups;
  • Eloundou et al.’s beta, rated by GPT-4, averaged from O*NET occupations to SOC codes (Eloundou et al. 2024);
  • Felten, Raj and Seamans’s AIOE (Felten et al. 2021). The AIOE repository states no licence, so AIOE appears only in aggregate statistics and never for a single occupation.

Employment. Employment weights come from ABS Labour Force table EQ08 (Australian Bureau of Statistics 2026b). It gives employed persons by ANZSCO v1.2 unit group, sex and state each quarter. The weights average the 4 quarters from May 2025 to February 2026: 14.67 million people employed, 1.66 million of them in Western Australia. EQ08 was the final release under that title. ABS has said the table is not published from April 2026 (Australian Bureau of Statistics 2026d), and Labour Force occupation data are coded to OSCA from the September 2026 reference period (Australian Bureau of Statistics 2026c). Neither source states whether unit-group detail will be published.

Earnings. Units are ranked by average weekly total cash earnings of all employees in the ABS Employee Earnings and Hours survey, May 2025 (data cube 11) (Australian Bureau of Statistics 2026a). No EEH cube gives hourly earnings at unit-group level. Two alternative rankings are reported:

  • average hourly total cash earnings of full-time non-managerial adult employees (EEH cube 13, published only for three-digit minor groups);
  • average salary or wage income from ATO Taxation Statistics 2023-24, Table 15B (Australian Taxation Office, n.d.).

EEH excludes owner-managers; EQ08 counts everyone employed.

Crosswalks. US occupations are linked to ANZSCO through BLS and ABS concordances: SOC 2018 to SOC 2010, SOC 2010 to ISCO-08, and ISCO-08 to ANZSCO v1.2. A fourth weighting scheme uses Jobs and Skills Australia’s direct correspondence from ANZSCO v1.2 to O*NET-SOC 2019, an archived copy (Jobs and Skills Australia, n.d.). Within each unit, US occupations are weighted by employment in the BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics for May 2025 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, n.d.).

Every file’s source, access date, checksum and licence are recorded in data/raw/MANIFEST.csv.

3 Methods

3.1 Edition spine

The analysis unit is the ANZSCO v1.2 unit group, because employment by sex and state is published only in that edition. There are 358 unit groups.

  • nfd codes. Employment coded only to a broader group (“not further defined”) is shared among the unit groups under it, in proportion to their employment in the same quarter, sex and state. These codes hold between 1.8% and 2.6% of employment in each quarter.
  • ANZSCO v1.3. It has exactly the same codes as v1.2, so it needs no bridge.
  • ANZSCO 2021 and 2022. EEH and ATO use these editions. They are brought back to v1.2 through the ABS correspondence tables. Of the 369 unit-to-unit links, 337 keep the same code, 5 are recoded, 14 merge several units into one, 7 split one unit across several and 6 are many-to-many.
  • Merges and splits. A v1.2 unit fed by several newer units takes their mean, weighted by ATO individual counts. A newer unit split across several v1.2 units passes its value to each.
  • Missing earnings. Units with no published EEH value after bridging (19 units) take the employment-weighted mean of their published siblings in the same minor group. Each one is listed in the appendix.

3.2 Usage-based exposure for each unit (method A)

The usage-based exposure of unit \(a\) is

\[ e_a = \sum_{s \in S_a} w_{as}\, e_s, \qquad \sum_{s \in S_a} w_{as} = 1, \]

where \(S_a\) is the set of linked US occupations with a non-missing score, and the weights are renormalised over that set. The extensive margin applies the same weights to an indicator of any measured use, \(\sum_s w_{as}\,\mathbf{1}[e_s > 0]\). Intensity is exposure divided by the extensive margin.

Four weighting schemes give four versions of every unit value:

  1. OEWS employment weights on the primary chain. This is the primary scheme.
  2. Equal weights on the same links.
  3. Title-match-first. For each ANZSCO occupation, only US occupations whose titles match are kept if any match; otherwise all its links are kept. 150 occupations in 81 units have a match.
  4. The JSA correspondence links, with OEWS weights. They cover 354 units.

The primary chain gives 2,438 unit-to-occupation links through 429 ISCO-08 units. Because ISCO-08 is coarser than both SOC and ANZSCO, the chain smooths zeros into small positive values. Every unit is therefore graded by how many US occupations feed it:

Grade Linked US occupations Units Share of employment
One-to-one one 59 13.5%
Few-to-one two to four 155 47.1%
Diffuse five or more 141 38.5%

Every headline result is rerun on non-diffuse units only.

A second chain, through the ANZSCO 2022 correspondence to ISCO-08, gives identical links for 350 units and different links for 8; the appendix lists them. Coverage is the share of employment in units with at least one scored US occupation. It is 99.1%, against a target set in advance of 98%. The 3 unmatched units are listed in the appendix.

3.3 Earnings deciles and concentration (method B)

  • Deciles. Units are ranked by earnings and cut into employment-weighted deciles, so each decile holds a tenth of employment. A unit whose employment straddles a boundary is split between deciles in proportion. Decile means are employment-weighted. Decile intensity is mean exposure divided by mean extensive margin.
  • Top minus bottom. The difference between the top and bottom deciles is reported in percentage points, never as a ratio.
  • Concentration index. \(CI = 2\,\mathrm{cov}(e, r)/\bar{e}\), with employment weights, where \(r\) is the employment-weighted fractional earnings rank. A positive index means exposure is concentrated among higher earners. It is not reported for AIOE, which is a standardised score with negative values.
  • Sensitivity runs. Results are rerun excluding units whose EEH relative standard error is above 25% (25 units). They are also rerun excluding a draft list of 13 owner-operator units. ABS publishes form of employment only by occupation major group (Australian Bureau of Statistics 2025), so the list is a judgement.

3.4 Usage against potential (method C)

For each unit, the usage-potential gap is the percentile rank of usage-based exposure minus the percentile rank of the potential measure.

  • Ranks are employment-weighted, and tied values share the mid-rank. In particular, every unit with zero usage-based exposure shares one rank.
  • Unit gaps are averaged within deciles, with employment weights.
  • A version using weighted z-scores is a check.
  • The comparison with Eloundou beta is partly mechanical, because usage-based exposure is itself gated on that beta. It compares use with feasibility inside the same task frame. JSA’s scores and AIOE are the independent checks, and JSA automation is the primary comparator.
  • The note also reports employment-weighted rank correlations, and the fifteen largest rank disagreements with JSA whose sign is the same under all four schemes.

3.5 Women and men, Western Australia, and usage by occupation group (method D)

  • Women and men. Deciles come from the persons earnings ranking. Within each decile, exposure is averaged with each sex’s employment.
  • Western Australia. The difference between WA and national mean exposure is \[\Delta = \sum_a (s^{WA}_a - s^{AUS}_a)\, e_a,\] where \(s\) are employment shares. By construction it reflects occupation mix only, since every unit carries one national value. The difference is split by major and sub-major group. Sub-major groups with fewer than five thousand WA workers are not shown separately. No WA by sex results are produced.
  • Usage by occupation group (Section 4.6). Each SOC major group’s share of Claude.ai conversations is divided by its share of employment.
    • For Australia and WA, employment is EQ08 allocated to SOC groups with the scheme 1 weights.
    • For the global row, it is US OEWS employment, because no global employment by SOC exists.

3.6 What counts as holding

These rules were fixed before any results were produced.

  • Decile profiles. A profile holds under a variant if its OLS slope across deciles has the same sign as the primary profile, and the Spearman correlation of the two sets of decile means is at least 0.7.
  • The gap. The gap holds if its sign in the top and bottom quintiles is the same under every weighting scheme.
  • Reporting. Every specification is reported, including those that do not hold. There are 48: four schemes, four samples and three earnings rankings.

4.7 Robustness

Of the 48 specifications, 27 hold against the primary profile under the rule above. Under scheme 4, 2 of 12 hold. One unit accounts for this: Sales Assistants (General), which has 3.9% of employment, most of it in the bottom decile. Under scheme 4 it links only to US Retail Salespersons, one of the score’s known artefacts. Leaving it out moves the scheme 4 top-minus-bottom difference from -2.4 pp to +7.7 pp. This check was added after the first results were seen, and is reported as such. The full sensitivity table is in the appendix.

5 Limitations

The usage data come from one product and its users. Claude.ai and Anthropic’s API serve a self-selected group of users. JSA reports that Claude.ai has under three per cent of Australian market share (Jobs and Skills Australia 2025, 35–36). Usage-based scores built from one platform mix how applicable AI is to a task with who happens to use that platform (Yin and Ogut 2026). Nothing in the note measures how Australian workers in a given occupation use AI.

Tasks, not jobs. The source classifies the task in each conversation, not the job of the person having it. A conversation about nutrition is not evidence that a nutritionist was involved. The Australian rows used in Section 4.6 carry the same caveat.

Zeros and gates. Over half of the scored US occupations have a score of exactly zero. A zero can mean the occupation’s tasks fell below the usage gate in Anthropic’s sample, or that its used tasks failed the capability gate. Because of that gate, the comparison with Eloundou beta is partly mechanical.

Known artefacts. Some scores sit oddly beside related occupations:

US occupation Score Related occupation Score
Legal Secretaries and Administrative Assistants zero Paralegals and Legal Assistants positive
Bartenders zero
Retail Salespersons higher Lawyers lower

These pass through the crosswalk unchanged. The Retail Salespersons score dominates the result for Sales Assistants (General) under scheme 4.

Crosswalk smoothing. The primary chain passes through ISCO-08, which is coarser than either end. Units fed by five or more US occupations hold 38.5% of employment. Results on non-diffuse units are reported beside the main results in the appendix.

Earnings. Ranking by earnings needs a few compromises:

  • Weekly earnings mix hourly pay with hours worked. No hourly earnings are published at unit-group level.
  • EEH leaves out owner-managers, while EQ08 counts them.
  • 19 units have no published EEH value and take their minor group’s mean. 25 units have relative standard errors above 25%.
  • In the ATO data, 23.1% of individuals have a blank or unclassifiable occupation code. Of these, 20.0% of all individuals are blank.

Sampling error. EQ08 publishes no standard errors. Unit-level employment, especially for Western Australia, is estimated with error that this note cannot show.

Timing. The four sources cover different periods:

Source Period
Usage-based scores Anthropic conversation samples collected before the score was published in March 2026
Australian usage shares April and May 2026
Employment May 2025 to February 2026
Earnings May 2025 (EEH) and 2023-24 (ATO)

Occupation-group shares. The published SOC major-group shares do not sum to one hundred per cent for any geography, even where all groups are published. The data documentation does not say what fills the gap.

What the note does not do. It describes; it does not estimate effects. It says nothing about employment, wages or hours responding to AI. It measures variation between occupations, not within them. It is not a forecast and not a job-loss or career-risk score.

6 What did not work, and changes along the way

  • The questions file. A separate file of research questions and choices was dropped on 25 October 2026. The method choices it would have held were logged in decision_log.md before any results were produced. The research question and framing were drafted after the first results.
  • Hourly earnings. These were the intended primary ranking but are not published at unit-group level. Weekly earnings are used instead.
  • Owner-managers. No unit-level data on owner-managers exist in published ABS tables, so that sensitivity run uses a judgement list.
  • The concentration index for AIOE was dropped, for the reason given in Section 3.
  • The JSA correspondence turned out to be coded to ANZSCO v1.2, not v1.3 as its archived web page implied.
  • Weighting scheme 4 does not reproduce the primary decile profile. The influence check that explains it was added after the results were seen.
  • The JSA automation gap does not keep its sign in the bottom quintile across schemes.

7 Contributions and AI use

Luc Taya chose the topic and data sources, made the judgement calls, edited the research question and framing, and wrote the interpretation, every takeaway and the theory box. Claude Code, an AI coding assistant, wrote the data pipeline under Luc’s direction and drafted the data, methods, limitations and appendix sections for Luc to edit. The data analysed are published by Anthropic, and the pipeline was written with Claude Code, an Anthropic product. Anthropic had no role in this project and has not reviewed or endorsed it.
